en: Now begins the first chapter of the Ṛgveda-Prātiśākhya.
Now begins the first chapter.
Now, the first chapter:
in the first chapter,
there are eight homogeneous vowels (samānākṣara) from the beginning, followed by four diphthongs (sandhyakṣara).

These vowels are indeed [five]; the short, long, and protracted [vowels], the anusvāra, or a consonant, or a vowel—whatever remains is all [consonants]. Among them, the first are the *sparśa* (stops), five of them; these constitute the five groups (*pañcavarga*).
There are four semivowels (*antasthā*), and after those, eight sibilants (*ūṣman*); of these, the last seven are voiceless (*aghoṣa*).

In each class [of consonants], the first and the third are voiced; the second and the fourth are aspirates; and the last is nasal. After that [nasal], at the end of a word, Gārgya prescribes the third [consonant of the class], while Śākaṭāyana prescribes the first.
Among the vowels, those with odd positions ending in the seventh (the short vowels) are short; the others are long. Both types, however, are syllables.
Those syllables which are heavy and long, as well as those followed by a conjunct consonant or an *anusvāra*, [are protracted].
(4) The *anusvāra* and a consonant are members of the preceding vowel; however, when there is another vowel in between, the consonants belong to the following one.
The *anusvāra* and the *visarjanīya* belong to the preceding vowel, or else, when followed by a conjunct consonant, they belong to both. (5) 1.
A short vowel has one *mātrā*, the interval between pauses (*avagraha*) is likewise; a long vowel is said to have two *mātrās*, and a protracted (*pluta*) vowel three.
For example: "Was it below? Was it above?"—in such cases, the protracted vowel is found three times, like a trembling fear.
A *svarabhakti* (vowel fragment) is a subordinate part of the preceding syllable; it is longer when it consists of one and a half *mātrās*, and otherwise [half a *mātrā*].
The other [vowels] are half [the duration] less; that which is known as *rakta* is nasal. A conjunction (*saṃyoga*), however, is the coming together of consonants.
(7) The letter *a* is guttural, as are the first and fifth [consonants of each class]. Some say these [letters] are chest-sounds (*urasya*).
The letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the sixth *ūṣman* (the sibilant *s*), the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the first class of consonants [are guttural]. (8)
The *e*-vowels, the *c*-class, the *i*-vowels, the *ai*-vowel, the letter *y*, and the letter *ś* are palatals (*tālavya*).
The retroflexes (*mūrdhanya*) are the *ṣ*-letter and the *ṭ*-class. The dental (*dantamūlīya*) is the *t*-class.
The letters *s*, *r*, and *l*—some say the letter *r* as well—are dental; the letter *v* is labial (*oṣṭhya*), except for the exceptions [to be mentioned].

"The nose, the nasal [consonants], and the *yama* and *anusvāra*—these are the places of articulation here; this is the instruction regarding the *yamas*. But the teacher Vedamitra says that the root of the tongue and the palate are the place of articulation for the letter *ḍa*;
and having come between these two vowels, that *ḍa* becomes the letter *la*."
That very same [consonant] becomes *ḍha*, and when joined with a sibilant (*ūṣman*), it is *ḍh*.
Examples here are *ilā* and *sālhā*; and *vīḍvaṅga* by means of the *avagraha*.
One should understand the exceptions mixed with these rules according to logic; the meaning of the entire treatise has been stated for every section.

In the instruction regarding the joining of places (sthāna-praśleṣa), when there is the substitution of short vowels for [long] vowels, both short and long vowels are considered homogeneous (savarṇa). That which is spoken with the thought "this is that" is called *taddhāva* (the state of being that); likewise are the *pādavats* (those like a quarter-verse) and the ritual commands (*praiṣas*).

And those words ending in a vowel occurring before the particle *iti*—provided they are not Vedic (*anārṣa*)—are treated as word-final (*padānta*), as are those joined with them, even in cases where they are not in *saṃhitā*.

And they utter these criticisms: "They are under the power of the *sāman*, for they apply the rules of the *pāda-pāṭha* to the *saṃhitā*; and they treat the *padya* verses like prose (*pada*) except when there is no substitution, [ignoring] the *nata*, *upācarita*, *krama*, and *svara* accents.
The teachers say that the first eight vowels at the end of a word are nasalized (*anunāsika*), provided they are not *pragṛhya*.
In that regard, the teachers demonstrate these three [rules] as the means for preventing the loss of the scriptural tradition:
The ten vowels beginning with *ṛ* are called "named" (*nāman*). In the case of prostration (*nati*), the preceding vowel is the object of prostration, while the subsequent one is the agent.

A vowel followed by a consonant (*upadha*) and marked with the *ari* (the *ṛ*-vowel) is like a single syllable when followed by a vowel or a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) consonant; such is the *visarjanīya*. (16–17)

The syllable *o* arising from a vocative, a *pragṛhya* vowel, a word not ending in another word, and the three [words] beginning with *ṣaṣṭha* that end in dual forms, as well as the two long vowels *sāpta* and *ātraka*, are *pragṛhya*. Furthermore, *asme*, *yuṣme*, *tve*, and *amī* are also *pragṛhya*; however, the penultimate [syllable] of these is not unaccented (*anudātta*) when it occurs at the end of a verse-line (*padya*).

The syllable *u*, when joined with the particle *iti*, is nasalized (*rākta*), unjoined (*apukta*), and lengthened according to the Śākala school. The fifth [nasal] following a spirant (*ūṣman*) and preceded by a guttural nasal (*nāmipūrva*) is likewise, except for the word *mahaḥ*. The others are as previously stated. A word ending in a vowel is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*) in the interval between words; in the opposite case, it is accented on the penultimate. Furthermore, before a stop (*sparśa*), a spirant (*ūṣman*) belonging to the preceding word [is nasalized]. 19–20.4.
In the morning, the word *devam* has an acute (*udātta*) accent on the syllable *bhā*, while the following syllable *va* is grave (*anudātta*). You have not abandoned that; it belongs to *adaḥ*.

The forms *staḥ* and *prāgātham* belong to *etaśe*. To *kardive*, the suffix *kar* is applied preceded by *apa-skarat-sāra-vi*. The word *astaḥ* [ends with] *svar*, which is circumflex (*svarita*), provided it is not part of a compound and follows a vowel-substitution (*svarādeśa*) where the preceding word does not end in *mahas*.
At the end of the *anargharcā* [meter], the following rules apply: the *svaraghoṣavat* [type of *udhna*] is not permitted after *repha*. In the case of *aruṣāsaḥ*, they did not satisfy the earth.

(22) In the *pathyā* [meter], when there is a single *pāda* containing the sequence "vara-vara-ava," and when it is joined with a compound member preceded by *vyapa* or *araya*, the *maghonī* [type of *divi*] occurs. In the *made* [meter], the first [syllable] is not followed by *arciṣātītṛṣām* in the subsequent [feet]. (23)
O Hotṛ, O Sanitar, O Potar, O Neṣṭar, O Sotar, O Savitar, O Netar, O Tvaṣṭar!
O Mātar, O Janitar, O Bhrātar, O Trātar, O Sthātar, O Jaritar, O Dhātar, O Dhartaḥ! O Jāmātṛ, O Duhiṭṛ, O Dartaḥ, O Praśāstar, O Avitaḥ, O Pitaḥ!

May he, who is the protector of those who have overcome faults, who moves with supreme vigor, who sustains the burden of the earth, the bestower of boons, the shatterer of the wicked, the one who awakens from the dust of worldly existence,
who repeatedly wards off the enemy, who possesses splendor, and who is the lord of the Sabaras— may he protect us.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Ṛgvedaprātiśākhya*.
Now begins the second chapter.

That which occurs when one joins the end of a word with the beginning of a word, such that the nature of the words remains conjoined, is *saṃhitā*. However, when there is a change of vowel without an interval of time, that is *vivṛtti*; it has the duration of a *svarabhakti*.
The rules for modification apply only to the ends and beginnings of words when those words are perceived as complete units, because of the brevity of the instruction.
A single phoneme that is joined [with another] is like the end of one word and the beginning of the next; it is to be understood according to the sequence of the vowels.

When *eṣa*, *khya*, and *sa* are preceded by vowels and followed by a consonant, they are called "consonant-joined" (*sadhīn*) with respect to the following syllable. They are "in direct order" (*anuloma*), while in the reverse case, they are "in inverse order" (*pratiloma*). || 2–3 ||
In that regard, the first and third [syllables] are elided among the reversals, but not among the others;
the sibilant (*ūṣman*) is dropped for three [syllables], except for those where they are vowels, and where those [reversals] do not occur in the verses.
[The hymn] *puraetā* [is recited] with the *titaunā* [verse], the *prauga* [hymn] with praises and eulogies.
The internal pause (*antaḥ-pada*) consists of the *vivṛtti* (separation); other than this, [the pauses] occur at word-junctions (*pada-saṃdhi*).
When two vowels of the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) are joined, they become a single long vowel.
An *i*-vowel followed by an *e*-vowel becomes *ai*, and likewise an *a*-vowel followed by an *o*-vowel becomes *au*.

The vowel *u* becomes *o* before other vowels; *e* occurs between *o* and *j*; and *au* occurs between *g* and *v*. These are called "contracted" (*praśliṣṭa*) sandhis. [Furthermore,] a homogeneous vowel becomes a semi-vowel (*antasthā*) of its own class when followed by a vowel produced from the same place of articulation (*svakaṇṭhya*).

Those [consonants] which have their own corresponding vowels are *kṣaipra* when they arise from a natural (*prākṛta*) vowel. 8. A *visarjanīya* not followed by *r*, preceded by a long vowel, and having a vowel as its following sound, as well as the letter *ā* and the last two vowels—these are the *padakrama* [cases]. 9.

When preceded by a short vowel, that [syllable] is the *akāra*; when preceded by the two vowels nearest to the end (the penultimate), they are the *udgrāha*. These are characterized by long vowels and function as the basis for the *udyāha* phrase.
In the case of the labial and palatal [vowels], the *vakāra* is inserted between them with a bent mind.
When the syllable *ṛ* follows, the guttural vowel *a* is used as its *udgrāha*.
(11) The original forms of the *udgrāhas* are [placed] before the vowel *a*; by nature, two become one, with the first being *o*.
These are the *padavṛttis* of the Easterners and the Pañcālas; among them, those of the Pañcālas have the labial vowel *u* preceding. (12)
Now, when combined with these natural and modified [vowels], the initial *a* of the quarter-verse becomes one; these are the results produced by euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).
If there is an *a* within the quarter-verse in the *saṃhitā*, it is light after a light [syllable].

The syllable beginning with *ya* may be supreme, or it may begin with *va*; likewise, it may be joined with another [consonant] when followed by a vowel at its end. When combined with suffixes ending in *-aye*, *-ayo*, *-ave*, or *-ava*, the letter *a* occurs in every way. (14–15)
And by this very [word] *va*, and not by anything else—O wondrous one, who is like Savitṛ? By all these steps that have been placed down, the subsequent [verses] arise.
Adāt, avarttaḥ, ajanayanta, avyatyāḥ, abhedayaḥ, apāṣṭiḥ, avantu, avīratā.
"From the state of 'mine-ness' he has released us; we have escaped from the skin, from the arrow, from the chariotless ones.

(17) "O Vāyu, for the all-conquering one, the Kavaṣas [sing]; the roaring one, swift as thought, self-sustained, the upholder of Truth, the kinsman, the golden-horned one"—thus with the *upadhā* bricks. (18)
Those who are masters of wealth—let not the serpent harm us here, O Agni.
Being born, O Agni, you became this; O dancer, you carry us across distress.
19. Crushing the serpent, the Maruts, following the nourishing one, seeking food, were born upon the path.

In the slaying of Vṛtra, in the battle, the Maruts, not tiring, rejoiced; they shouted aloud on every side. (20) They speak as if for the sake of protection; it has been told to me: they have bestowed gifts, they have placed [them] in Agni; Nahuṣa shattered our fortresses. O Dawn, I have established thee; this Yama carries thee away; Aditi [is the mother] of birth; through her, prosperity has been attained according to the path. (21)
The people have followed for the sake of his body; being virtuous, they have cast away their reproaches in the sky.
Bearing [offerings], seeking protection, let there be protection from the baseless one; let the goat of the magician be cast down.
O Lord of abundant wealth, slayer of the Asuras, the white and ruddy one has become manifest; by him may we be protected today.
Those who were sisters, they became speakers upon the dry wood; they grew strong with their dust-covered seats.
The benevolent ones generated the archers’ adversaries; O Agni, burn away from the mind those who [obstruct] the path.
Those who found your prayer through austerity, those who [attained] his foot, the Brahmin who surpassed him, and he who led him away.
So, from those hates of ours caused by others, I have made [the waters] full of milk and immortal.
One is near, and another at the rising of the sun; the son is both in the distance and from afar.
Within the foot is the bird, and in the mid-air is the bird; you have loosened his three weapons.
O Aśvins, both [of you] bestowed glory upon Śaryāta from the Sṛñjaya clan, as did the kinsmen upon Śayu from the Andhas clan; [they bestowed] milk.

(26) Those words beginning with *iti* after a root-form (*prakṛti*), and the first [vowel] in a vocative case (*āṣyām*) before vowels, are *pragṛhya* as previously stated. Those [vocatives] followed by a vowel (*sahodayaḥ*) are *pragṛhīta* words; however, those ending in three syllables are not *pragṛhya* in all cases. (27)
In the *ārṣī* [sandhi], the suffix beginning with the vowel *u* is preceded by the letter *a* due to its opening (*vivṛtti*).
When it begins with *ū*, there is the word *svit*; when it is the letter *a*, as in *pūṣā*, it is not so provided it is preceded by a monosyllabic word. [The examples are:
*śraddhā*, *samrājñī*, *suśamī*, *svadhautī*, *pṛthujrayī*, *pṛthivīṣā*, and *manīṣā*.

The word *ayā* [is unelided] before *nidrā*, *jyā*, *pra*, and *eti*; likewise when it occurs before the vowels *svarāṇām*, *mukhye*, *pare*, and the fifth and sixth vowels (*u* and *ū*). When preceded by *sa*, the word *ca* [is unelided] at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pādādau*) or when followed by a vowel (*udaye*). Words ending in *ṣ* [are unelided] before *joṣam*, *carṣaṇi*, and *carṣaṇibhyaḥ*. Words ending in *e* [are unelided] before *mitrayoḥ*, *asmadī*, and *van*. The word *namasyuḥ*, when its penultimate letter is *i* (*upadham*), and other words consisting of a single consonant (*apṛktam*) [are also unelided]. 29–30.6.
In the *Gotama* [Anuvāka], the two gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*) followed by *e* and *o* are elided before *luśa*; likewise in *aminanta*.
In the case of *vibhvā*, *vidhartā*, *vipanyā*, and *kadā yā mātā*, even when the vowel *ṛ* occurs at the beginning of a word, it is elided.
In the *Parucchepa* [Anuvāka], the vowel *a* in *bhīṣā patha* is elided, and in the three instances of *amimatriṣu*, the preceding vowel is protracted (*pluta*).
The suffixes *sa*, etc., which have been prescribed as substitutes [for *tad*], when preceded by a protracted vowel (*pluta*) or an anusvāra, [are used] as follows:
*sedu*, *sāsmin*, *semabhi*, *sābhi-vegaḥ*, *sedṛ-bhavaḥ*, *sopamā*, *sauṣadhīr-anu*, *sāsmā-aram*, *sota-naḥ*, *sendra*, *viśvā-seti*, *sāsmākam*, *anavadya-sāsi*. 32–33.
May Agni be with us here; may he be with the Vasiṣṭhas; may he be with our own people; may he be with these men.
May he win these, may he win this, may he win those, may he win these; may he rule over these, may he rule over those. 34.
Now indeed, thus upon your woolly back, upon us, on the place of sacrifice—your garment.
O you who dwell in the sacred hearths, even now turn your feet elsewhere; let Indra not come hither.
He has raised up the impetuous wealth for the one with a hundred rays, for the one with ten arms, for the one with ten arms.
Just as you have gladdened and just as you have shone upon the one with ten arms, so bring forth the light; drink this, O rider of the chariot!
These heroes have gone forth; they have made him [the sun] so that he may cross over these two worlds like ships.
They move swiftly through the desert-like expanse, active and together, like firm wheels or like two steeds rushing toward the prize.
Like the Aśvins, they are the observers of those clothed in thick garments; they are like the great Ādityas or the dawns.
"Sing praise to the Mother so that she may release [the waters] to flow; O Indra, together with her on the woolly ridge, you have established your own power.
(38) "The two who possess cattle as their ornament, the two who urge on the cattle, the two who proclaim [the truth]—with inspired thought, both Earth and Heaven [have come] to you.
(39) "With inspired thought, seeking aid, they have caused delight here; like two great ones, according to what was received. (39)
He has closed off the womb with a hundred bolts;
he strikes down the false deceiver who has mounted there weaponless while others are armed.
He has driven the non-existent out from here; who indeed has struck back at the non-existent?
The god Aṅgiras covered him; he pierced him and joined him [to life]. 41.
The slayer of the serpent cleared the path; the two [heaven and earth] were yoked by the one who brings joy.
Having seized the inheritance, he yoked Kuruśravaṇa; I have covered him. 42.
The examples *śunaś cic chepam*, *niditam narā*, *vā śaṃsam pūṣaṇam*, and *narā ca śaṃsam daivyam* are those that are not joined according to the sequence [of the rules].
Where there is a long vowel, there the *vivṛtti* (separation) is long; however, when there are two junctions (*dvisandhi*), the vowels on both sides are *svarita*.
The Prācyas, Pañcālas, and those from Upadhāna are the followers of Śākalya the Elder; others have a different tradition.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Ṛgvedaprātiśākhya*; here begins the third chapter.
Now begins the third chapter:

Acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (svarita)—these are the three tones. They are said to depend upon the syllable through stretching (āyāma), relaxation (viśrāma), and projection (ākṣepa).
In the case of the merging of two monophthongs (*ekākṣara-samāveśa*), the accent of the former [vowel] is *svarita*.
Of that *svarita*, the portion higher than the acute (*udātta*) is either half a *mātrā* or even a quarter *mātrā*.
The remaining subsequent portion is *anudātta*; however, if it is not heard as acute (*udātta-śruti*), it is so.
Sometimes a syllable is called *udātta*, and sometimes another following it is *svarita*. When a syllable preceded by an *udātta* within a word is *anudātta*, it is *svarita*.
Other than this, they call the *svarita* occurring in a word "natural" (*jātya*).
One should know that the supreme syllable is higher than both [the udātta and anudātta]; it is the udātta syllable resulting from their combination.
Even if there are many anudātta syllables, provided they do not precede a preceding udātta, [the result is as follows]:
when there is a unification with an udātta, the resulting combined (sandhi) syllable is udātta.
Furthermore, when a following syllable is unaccented (anudātta), one should apply the circumflex (svarita) accent if the preceding syllable is also circumflex (svarita).

This same rule applies in cases of elision (praśleṣa) between two *i*-sounds, in the *kṣaipra* and *abhinihita* circumflex accents, and in the *ruṣa* accents where the preceding syllable is acute (*udātta*); according to Śākalya, one should act in this manner.
Māṇḍūkeya maintains that one should remember this for all joined vowels (*praśliṣṭa*):
"The properties of those [vowels] that arise later become unified with those that arise first.
This is certain when preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*), whether by means of a hiatus (*vivṛtti*) or a consonant.
If an elided vowel is not followed by an udātta or a svarita accent, it is marked as svarita.

They designate these separately as the six types of *svarita*: *vaivṛtta*, *tairovyañjana*, *kṣaipra*, *abhinihita*, *praśliṣṭa*, and that which occurs according to the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).
After a *svarita* vowel, there occurs the *pracaya* accent for the following *anudātta* vowels;
one, two, or many of these attain the quality of being heard as *udātta*.
Some, however, restrict this to one or several syllables at the very end.
Or rather, that which remains after [the application of] *niyukta* has an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent following it.
Some hold that this restriction is due to a specific cause and possesses the properties of the *pracaya* accent;
the *pracaya* accent is the usage of Śākalya and Ātreyeya. (12–13)

However, in the case of *parigraha*, [the rule applies] after that which does not end in an archaic (*ārṣa*) vowel and after that which has been reduced to a single syllable; for others, the practice is *nyāsa*. If those two are vowels followed by another vowel, then, just as in the case of vowels being joined together and becoming one, [the same rule applies].
One should understand it to be taught thus regarding the separation (avagraha) of syllables:
[the first part] is like a word-end, while the subsequent parts of the *padya* and so forth are treated as if they were not in *saṃhitā* when they are doubly-accented (*dvyudātta*).
Or, like the *jātya* accent, it is so at the end; likewise for *tanū* and *śacī* following the two preceding [words].

In the case of the two subsequent three-mora [syllables], even the final one is a *pracaya-svara*; according to some, the morae are placed on the lower [pitch]. Vyāḷi [holds that] both [preceding syllables] are *samasvara*.
One should pronounce the vowels without ambiguity, neither drawn out nor trembling.
One should not suppress a *svarita* accent, nor should one excessively alter the two preceding [vowels].
The *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and the *praśliṣṭa*—these *svarita*s vibrate when they are followed by a high-pitched (*udātta*) or a *svarita* vowel. (18–19)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Ṛgvedaprātiśākhya*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

The preceding consonants (sparśas) and the following sibilants (vyañjanas) are established as the inevitable substitutes for those [consonants] that have been positioned [in the following positions]. When followed by voiced sounds (ghoṣavat), the first and third [consonants of each class] substitute for their own respective last [consonants] when they arise after the last [consonants]. The letter *ś* is substituted by *ch* according to Śākalya’s father when it is preceded by any of the first [consonants].
By those same [consonants] at the end of a word, which have become the third [in their respective classes], there is the emergence of the fourth as the letter *ha*.
In the place of *vi* (*visarga*), when a contact consonant (*sparśa*) emerges, there is the letter *ma*; this is the supreme self of the emergence of all [consonants].
Among the semivowels (*antasthā*), excluding *ra*, and among the following [sibilants], one should apply the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form of each respective [consonant] at the beginning of a word.
Likewise, when *n* arises after *m*, it becomes *ñ*, except when followed by *ś* or *c*.

When *t* arises after *j* or *l*, they become palatals (*tālavya*). When a voiceless sound (*aghoṣa*) follows, *t* becomes *c*. When those two arise after *ch*, it becomes *ś*; however, according to Śākalya, this does not occur. These are the *vaśaṅgama* [conversions].
They say that when *r* and a sibilant (*ūṣman*) arise, the letter *m* becomes an *anusvāra*, which is their falling away.
(5) Some say that when followed by a voiceless sibilant, it becomes *ṅ*; others say it becomes *k* after *ṭ* and *n*.
They say it becomes *t* when followed by the arising of *s*, and *c* when followed by *ś* after *ñ*. (6)
This is the rule for those [consonants] included within [the preceding groups], which end in sibilants (ūṣman) and have not formed a saṃhitā, in this chapter.
By the expansion of *cit*, there is the disappearance of *uṣman*; [the word] *kakudmān* has the sound *satvāṭ*, which is a refutation of those who are fallen.
7 The *visarjanīya* becomes *ākāra* when followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*) and lacking *repha*;
[the words] *okāra* and *hrasvapūrva*—these two are fixed in their euphonic combinations (*sandhi*) as they are pronounced. 8
When followed by a vowel or a voiced sound, every *upadhmānīya* becomes *repha*; however, when followed by another *repha*, the rules for *repha*-sandhi apply again.
A *repha* that arises [after an *upadhmānīya*] is elided, and its penultimate vowel is lengthened; this rule applies to both short and long vowels.
When followed by an unvoiced sound, both the *rephin* and the non-*rephin* [anusvāra] become a sibilant (*ūṣman*) if a stop (*sparśa*) follows.

A consonant preceded by a vowel or an *anusvāra* is pronounced twice when it is the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*). This is the rule for sequential pronunciation (*krama*), except in cases where there is no sequence. However, an aspirated consonant (*soṣman*) is pronounced once together with its preceding [unaspirated] counterpart. A consonant that is not the first member of a conjunct is also pronounced once with its own [aspirated] counterpart, provided it follows the letter *cha*, the letter *ra*, a stop (*sparśa*), or the letter *la*; or it occurs after an aspirate (*ūṣman*) and is not followed by a vowel. The letter *ra* is not doubled when it is separated from the preceding vowel by a labial (*uṣṭhya*), nor when it is a non-initial consonant (*anupadha*) followed by a vowel or an aspirate. Furthermore, the letter *pa* is not doubled when followed by *va*, *ma*, or *ya*, nor when it is the initial of a word (*padādi*) followed by two *ta*s or *ne*. The letter *cha* is not doubled when joined with a long vowel, except in the case of the word *meti*. Finally, a consonant is not doubled according to the *Śākala* school's rule when it is joined with another consonant.
